---
title: "Reading the outputs"
subtitle: "Find the generated climate series, model responses, and indicators"
---

Run products live under the configured `project_dir`. For production projects,
use a directory outside the toolbox checkout.

## The layout

```text
<project_dir>/
  config/runs/                   configuration and run records
  data/spatial/                  basin geometry, locations and maps
  data/climate/                  historical forcing and projection products
  models/hydrology/wflow/         model, historical run and evaluation
  scenarios/_engine/requests/<request_id>/  scenario generation settings
  scenarios/_engine/collections/<id>/
    collection.json              collection inventory
  scenarios/<id>/                generated climate series
    scenario_run_lookup.csv      generated series and their relationships
    perturbation_lookup.csv      monthly temperature and precipitation changes
    series/run_<run_id>.nc        generated climate series
  experiments/<name>/
    _engine/simulation.json      simulation settings used
    hydrology/wflow/output/      retained model responses
    _engine/metric_sets/<id>/
      metrics.json              indicator definitions and source records
      return_level_benchmark.json  scope of return-level checks
    results/metric_sets/<id>/
      metric_run_lookup.csv     links indicator rows to simulations
      <token>_indicators.csv     metric,location,run_group_id,value
  logs/
  benchmarks/
```

Two experiments can use the same generated climate series, but each experiment
keeps its own model responses and indicators. To relate an indicator to the
climate change that produced it, match its `run_group_id` to `metric_run_lookup.csv`, then
match its `run_id` to `scenario_run_lookup.csv`, then its `st_id` to
`perturbation_lookup.csv`.
The scenario with an empty `st_id` is the unperturbed reference case.

## Check whether a run finished

Look under `logs/` for each workflow's messages. Scenario generation writes
`logs/wf3_generate_scenarios_<plan_key>.log`; simulation writes
`logs/wf4_simulate_system_<experiment>.log`. The `benchmarks/` directory
records the time and resource use of individual steps.

`<plan_key>` matches the name of the corresponding directory under
`scenarios/_engine/requests/`. An incomplete run can leave logs and partial files.
Check `collection.json` or `metrics.json` in the corresponding `_engine/`
metadata directory before treating a collection or
indicator set as complete.

The runners record each attempt under `config/runs/_engine/invocations/`,
including failed runs and dry runs. These records help diagnose a run; they do
not establish that its results are complete.

## Reading a metric set

Read `experiments/<name>/_engine/metric_sets/<id>/metrics.json` before
its tables. It identifies the
indicators, the model responses they came from, and the files in the set.

Some indicators have one value per simulation. Return levels are fitted from
groups of simulations; wet- and dry-month indicators use a shared reference
month. The set records the group members and reference location. Numerical
values are stored to four significant digits, so retain the underlying model
responses if you need more detailed analysis.

### Opening a metric table in Excel

`run_group_id` in `<token>_indicators.csv`, and `run_group_id` and `run_id` in
`metric_run_lookup.csv`, are **fixed-width zero-padded text**, not numbers. With a
collection of 10 or more runs they read `01`, `02`, ...; with 100 or more,
`001`. The width is a property of the collection's capacity, and the padding is
what makes the id joinable.

Excel converts them to numbers on a plain double-click, dropping the padding and
turning `01` into `1`. Microsoft 365 announces this in a "Data conversion"
notification; **older Excel does it silently.** Either way, a file re-saved
afterwards has lost the join key: `run_group_id` no longer matches `metric_run_lookup.csv`,
and the toolbox's own readers refuse the mismatch rather than guess which unit a
row means.

There is no way to write a CSV that prevents this. Excel's CSV parser ignores
quoting for type inference, so a file that Excel opens correctly on a
double-click is one that is no longer a plain CSV. Use one of these instead:

- **Import rather than open** (works everywhere, changes no settings). Excel →
  *Data* → *From Text/CSV* → *Transform Data*, set the `run_group_id` and
  `run_id` columns to *Text*, then *Close & Load*. This is the only route
  that is correct on every Excel version.
- **Turn the conversion off** (Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021+, per machine).
  *File* → *Options* → *Data* → *Automatic Data Conversion* → clear **"Remove
  leading zeros from numeric text and convert to a number"**. Double-click then
  works, but the setting does not travel with the file, so a collaborator opening
  the same table still needs it.
- **Read it in code**, preserving each table's identifiers explicitly. In
  pandas, use `pd.read_csv(path, dtype={"run_group_id": str})` for indicator
  tables, `dtype={"run_group_id": str, "run_id": str}` for the metric lookup,
  and `dtype={"run_id": str, "st_id": str}` for the scenario lookup. Read the
  perturbation lookup with `dtype={"st_id": str}`. `read_csv` with no dtype has
  the same failure mode as Excel.

If a table's ids have already been flattened, do not repair them by re-padding to
the width of the longest value --- that is a guess. Re-export the metric set, or
recover the file from the set, which is immutable.

## Return levels and their limits

Return levels are fitted from groups of simulated years with a GEV distribution.
Read `return_level_validation` in `metrics.json` before using them. It identifies
the return periods and conditions assessed by the supplied benchmark;
`return_level_benchmark.json` holds that assessment. The benchmark covers a
limited set of synthetic cases. It does not establish accuracy for your basin,
and the results have no uncertainty intervals. Treat these return levels as
screening indicators, not design estimates.

The recorded GEV parameters use SciPy's `(c, loc, scale)` convention. The shape
parameter often written as ξ is `-c`; check this sign when comparing fits with
another tool. Each fit also reports `shape_coverage`, including how far its
estimated `c` falls outside the shapes tested in the benchmark. A fit outside
that range has not been assessed by this benchmark. Small departures are not
strong evidence on their own because shape estimates from short records are
uncertain.

Keep a metric table together with its `metrics.json` and
`return_level_benchmark.json` when sharing or comparing return levels. The CSV
alone does not identify the estimator or its assessment.

## Are these outputs current?

Simulation checks that its requested scenario collection still matches the
current inputs. If the request is missing or out of date, the error names the
generation command to run. Simulation does not automatically choose a
collection. You can also name an existing collection explicitly in the
simulation settings file.

The `_engine/simulation.json` record ties an experiment to its collection,
model, and simulation settings. Use a new experiment name when those inputs
change. If you change only the indicators, `operation: metrics-only` creates a
new metric set from retained model responses without rerunning simulation.

For a reproducible comparison, keep the whole project output directory, not
only the indicator CSVs. The model build settings used by HydroMT are recorded
in `models/hydrology/wflow/hydromt_build_config.yml`.

See [Running the workflows](running.qmd) to calculate different indicators
from retained responses.
